replacement: 4. No armed force shall be allowed to pass for hostile purposes through the country of the contracting powers, or of the allies in their respective empires, or to go by sea, unless all the cities — that is to say, Athens, Argos, Mantinea and Elis — vote for such passage.

note: Adds an invented lead sentence "Each state is to take the oath as follows" that the source lacks.
replacement: The oath shall be taken at Athens by the Senate and the magistrates, and the Prytanes shall administer it. At Argos, the Senate, the Eighty and the Artynae take it, and the Eighty administer it. At Mantinea, the Demiurgi, the Senate and the other magistrates take it, and the Theori and Polemarchs administer it. At Elis, the Demiurgi, the magistrates and the Six Hundred take it, and the Demiurgi and the Thesmophylaces administer it. The oaths are to be renewed thirty days before the Olympic games, when the Athenians go to Elis, Mantinea and Argos, and ten days before the great feast of the Panathenaea, when the Argives, Mantineans and Eleans go to Athens. The articles of the treaty, the oaths and the alliance are to be inscribed on a stone pillar: by the Athenians in the citadel, by the Argives in the market-place, in the temple of Apollo, and by the Mantineans in the temple of Zeus, in the market-place. The cities are also to erect a brazen pillar jointly at the Olympic games now at hand. If the above cities see good to add anything to these articles, whatever all of them agree upon after consulting together shall be binding.

note: The word "surely" in the proposed oath was dropped.
replacement: This proposal was not accepted, so the Eleans tried a second. If the Lacedaemonians objected to restoring Lepreum, they should instead ascend the altar of the Olympian Zeus, since they were so anxious to have access to the temple, and swear before the Hellenes that they would surely pay the fine at a later day. This was also refused, and the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple, the sacrifice and the games, and sacrificed at home. The Lepreans were the only other Hellenes who did not attend. Still, the Eleans were afraid that the Lacedaemonians would sacrifice by force, and kept guard with a heavy-armed company of their young men. A thousand Argives and the same number of Mantineans joined them, along with some Athenian cavalry who stayed at Harpina during the feast. Great fears were felt in the assembly that the Lacedaemonians would come in arms, especially after Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been scourged on the course by the umpires. His horses had won, but the Boeotian people were proclaimed the victor, because he had no right to enter. So he came forward on the course and crowned the charioteer, to show that the chariot was his. After this incident all were more afraid than ever and firmly expected a disturbance. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet and let the feast pass by, as we have seen. After the Olympic games, the Argives and the allies went to Corinth to invite her to come over to them. They found some Lacedaemonian envoys there, and a long discussion followed, which ended in nothing, since an earthquake occurred and they dispersed to their different homes.

note: Adds an attribution ("say") the source does not have.
replacement: The next day the Argives and their allies drew up in the order in which they meant to fight if they happened to meet the enemy. The Lacedaemonians were coming back from the water to their old camp by the temple of Heracles. Suddenly they saw their adversaries right in front of them, all in perfect order and advanced from the hill. The Lacedaemonians do not remember ever having experienced a shock like this one. There was hardly any time to prepare. They fell into their ranks at once and in haste, with Agis, their king, directing everything as the law requires. When a king is in the field, every command comes from him. He gives the word to the Polemarchs, they pass it to the Lochages, these to the Pentecostyes, these again to the Enomotarchs, and these last to the Enomoties. All orders needed go the same way and quickly reach the troops. Almost the whole Lacedaemonian army, except for a small part, consists of officers under officers, so the responsibility for what is to be done falls on many.
